paper_title: ROLE OF ROOM SIZE AND INTERACTION DISTANCE ON STRESS-RELATED FEELINGS AND SOCIAL INTERACTION OF DYADS
venue: Master's Thesis, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
abstract: Eighty male and 80 female college students participated in an experiment to study reactions to stress as a function of room size and interaction distance. Two subjects (one male and one female) sat on stools either relatively close together (1.22m) or far apart (2.74m), in a waiting room relatively large 5.94m X 3.96m or small 2.44m X 3.96m. They completed a Personality and Environment questionnaire, received task instructions and consent forms, and then waited 10-min in the large or small room for the experimental task that involved receiving either shocks or lights as performance feedback. During the waiting period three observers watched through a one-way mirror and recorded specific behaviors of each of the subjects. After the 10-min wait, the Personality and Environment questionnaire was readministered as well as a sociometric questionnaire. The design was a factorial of 2(Stress Conditions) X 2 (Room Sizes) X 2(Seating Distances) X 2 (Sex of Subject) X 2(Assessment Times). Ten pairs of subjects were randomly assigned to one of the eight experimental conditions. The analysis of the three semantic differential items relating to current stress state (Rattled and Jittery vs Cool and Collected, Calm vs Worried, Tense vs Relaxed) indicated a significant Stress Condition X Seating Distance X Assessment Time interaction. That is, when anticipating the Shock Condition subjects showed a greater increase in stress feelings when they interacted Close than Far. No effects of sex nor room size on these stress ratings were observed. These findings supported the notion that interaction distance, and not room size, is the more prominent spatial variable associated with crowding effects.
methodology: A factorial design was used with 2 (Stress Conditions: Anticipated Shock vs No Shock) X 2 (Room Sizes: Large vs Small) X 2 (Seating Distances: Close vs Far) X 2 (Sex of Subject: Male vs Female) X 2 (Assessment Time: First vs Second Consecutive 5-min observation period). Subjects were paired (one male, one female) and randomly assigned to one of the eight between-subject conditions. Participants completed a Personality and Environment questionnaire before and after a 10-minute waiting period. During the waiting period, three observers watched through a one-way mirror and recorded specific behaviors using a checklist. A sociometric questionnaire was administered at the end of the session. The experimental task involved paired associate learning with either electric shocks (Anticipated Shock) or lights (No Shock) as feedback.
sample: 80 males and 80 females (N=160) college students enrolled in an introductory psychology course at Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University. 11 subjects were eliminated from experimental analysis due to knowing confederates, realizing they were being watched, or changing interpersonal distance. Analyses for some outcomes used N=115 (implied by df=114).

manipulated_features.details: Ceiling height was constant at 2.44m (8 ft). A removable partition was used to create the small room.
Distance between two subjects seated on stools.
Determined by task instructions: Anticipated Shock involved painful but harmless electric shocks as feedback; No Shock involved green/red lights as feedback.

measures: Verbalization (Experiment Avoidance, Experiment Other, Other/Non-experiment topics)
Composite Stress Score (Rattled and Jittery vs Cool and Collected, Calm vs Worried, Tense vs Relaxed)

outcomes.variable: Sociometric Ratings (Self-reported about partner, semantic differential)

key_findings.finding: Interaction distance, not room size, significantly influenced stress ratings.
key_findings.details: In the Anticipated Shock condition, subjects interacting at a close distance felt significantly more stressful than those at a far distance. No effects of sex or room size on stress ratings were observed.
key_findings.effect_size: Stress Condition X Seating Distance X Assessment Time interaction: F(1,114)=5.76, p<.02. Post-treatment differences due to seating distance were significant for Shock condition (p<.01).

key_findings.finding: Close seating distance increased talking and fidgeting.
key_findings.details: Subjects talked and fidgeted significantly more often in the Close condition than in the Far condition.
key_findings.effect_size: Talking: F(1,144)=6.49, p<.025 (Close mean=9.76, Far mean=7.35). Fidgeting: F(1,144)=5.63, p<.025 (Close mean=12.65, Far mean=10.78).

key_findings.finding: Body orientation towards partner decreased in close/stressful conditions.
key_findings.details: Subjects showed significantly more body orientation toward their partner in the Far rather than Close condition. For the Shock condition, body orientation decreased from the first to the second 5-min period.
key_findings.effect_size: Distance main effect: F(1,144)=6.44, p<.025 (Far mean=9.68, Close mean=7.24). Stress X Time Period interaction: F(1,114)=5.52, p<.025.

key_findings.finding: Confidence decreased only in the Anticipated Shock condition.
key_findings.details: Confidence ratings were reliably higher at the first assessment. A decrease in confidence occurred only for the Shock condition.
key_findings.effect_size: Stress condition X Assessment Time interaction: F(1,114)=8.82, p<.005 (Shock Pre=5.89, Post=5.10; No Shock Pre=5.86, Post=5.85).

key_findings.finding: Perceived confinement was influenced by both room size and seating distance.
key_findings.details: Subjects felt most confined when sitting far from their partner in the small room and most free when sitting close to their partner in the large room.
key_findings.effect_size: Room Size main effect: F(1,114)=4.93, p<.05. Seating Distance main effect: F(1,114)=4.07, p<.05.

key_findings.finding: Regret increased only in the Anticipated Shock condition.
key_findings.details: Subjects in the Anticipated Shock condition became more markedly regretful after the 10-min wait.
key_findings.effect_size: Stress condition X Assessment Time interaction: F(1,114)=16.53, p<.001 (Shock Pre=1.50, Post=2.86; No Shock Pre=1.92, Post=1.97).

key_findings.finding: Environmental pleasantness and attractiveness decreased under stress.
key_findings.details: Subjects in the Anticipated Shock condition rated the environment as reliably less pleasant and less attractive after the waiting period.
key_findings.effect_size: Unpleasantness (assessment time main effect): F(1,114)=5.52, p<.05. Attractiveness (stress condition main effect): F(1,114)=4.03, p<.05.

key_findings.finding: Roominess was primarily affected by room size, but also by stress condition over time.
key_findings.details: The large room was rated as markedly more roomy. The room appeared more roomy after the No Shock treatment.
key_findings.effect_size: Room Size main effect: F(1,114)=45.94, p<.001. Stress condition X Assessment Time interaction: F(1,114)=5.20, p<.05.

key_findings.finding: Comfort ratings showed a Room Size X Sex interaction.
key_findings.details: Males were more comfortable in the smaller room, while females rated the larger room as more comfortable.
key_findings.effect_size: Room Size X Sex interaction: F(1,114)=5.10, p<.05 (Males small room mean=4.84, large room mean=4.30; Females small room mean=4.45, large room mean=5.05).

key_findings.finding: Environment became more interesting over time, especially in small rooms and close distances.
key_findings.details: The environment was judged more interesting during the second assessment. This effect was intensified in the small room and close seating distance conditions.
key_findings.effect_size: Assessment time main effect: F(1,114)=17.59, p<.001. Room Size X Assessment Time: F(1,114)=4.40, p<.05. Seating Distance X Assessment Time: F(1,114)=5.74, p<.05.

key_findings.finding: Partners were perceived as more friendly, sociable, talkative, and outgoing in close seating arrangements.
key_findings.details: This effect was particularly pronounced in the small room for talkativeness and outgoingness.
key_findings.effect_size: Friendly (Seating Distance main effect): F(1,114)=7.62, p<.01. Sociable (Seating Distance main effect): F(1,114)=9.13, p<.01. Talkative (Seating Distance main effect): F(1,114)=8.88, p<.005. Outgoing (Seating Distance main effect): F(1,114)=11.34, p<.001. Talkative (Seating Distance X Room Size interaction): F(1,114)=7.91, p<.01. Outgoing (Seating Distance X Room Size interaction): F(1,114)=5.44, p<.025.

key_findings.finding: Partners were rated as more anxious in the Anticipated Shock condition.
key_findings.effect_size: Stress condition main effect: F(1,114)=6.55, p<.025.

theories_referenced: Equilibrium theory of intimacy (Argyle & Dean, 1965; Patterson, 1973)
mechanisms: Crowding (specifically close interaction distance) intensifies the individual's typical reaction to the situation (Freedman's theory).
Violation of personal space leads to arousal and stress.
Close proximity between people facilitates interpersonal communication.
Talking and fidgeting can be interpreted as nervous behavior or a way to distract oneself from stress.
Individuals protect their personal space zones under stress, leading to decreased body orientation towards others.
Compensatory changes in nonverbal intimacy (e.g., less direct body orientation) occur to restore equilibrium when physical proximity is high.
Stress feelings can generalize to perceptions of the environment, making it seem less pleasant or attractive.
Spatial restrictions imposed by walls can increase the perception of social distance and confinement.
limitations: The study did not find an expected influence of seating distance on the frequency of facial orientations, which was predicted by some theories (Patterson, Argyle & Dean).
The specific context of a waiting room for a psychology experiment might limit the generalizability of findings to other environments.
design_implications: Design waiting rooms (e.g., in hospitals, doctor's offices, airports, bus/subway stations) to minimize social interaction and ongoing anxiety feelings, especially in stressful contexts.
Maximize space between adjacent seats in anxiety-provoking waiting areas to reduce perceived closeness and potential stress.
Avoid fixed furniture arrangements (e.g., bolted chairs) that prevent individuals from regulating their interactive distance and moving freely.

Furniture design should be tailored to the function of the setting and user needs; more space between chairs may be desirable in doctor's waiting rooms, while less space might be acceptable in social lounges.
